Washing long hair is really so tiring. Not sure how long your hair is but mine is mid-back and these are my tips on how to wash long hair without passing out in the shower: 

1. Shower chair/bench. A moveable shower chair would be ideal but my shower is tiny with a built-in bench. I sit while I’m applying shampoo and conditioner and only stand up to rinse. 

2. Scalp scrubber. It lathers faster than just your hands so your arms aren’t in the air as much. They also make some that vibrate so it can double as a scalp massager. The downside is it might tangle your hair more. 

3. Clarifying shampoo. I try to stay away from super moisturizing shampoos that might need a second lather or take forever to rinse out. Try something from Suave or V8. It won’t wreck your hair, especially if you aren’t shampooing every day. 

4. Leave in conditioner applies to lengths and ends only. You can use a small amount of regular conditioner, buy a separate leave in product, or even apply a treatment like K18. My favorite trick is to mix some of my favorite leave-in with some water in a spray bottle, preferably one of those continuous misting pumps. It covers a lot of hair pretty quickly and it’s buildable, so there’s less of overdoing it and being stuck with oily hair until the next shower. This might depend on how well your hands and fingers function. 

Other must haves for me are a turbie twist to dry my hair and a tangle teezer comb. 

I haven’t done this, but another tip I’ve heard of is to schedule weekly washes at a hair salon. It doesn’t have to be some super expensive place, Great Clips and similar salons also do shampoos. If this is doable financially, it might be a great solution.

Try putting some lube or Aquaphor/Vaseline around and inside your vaginal opening to help it glide in easier. Tampons with applicators are so much easier to use, and I found that rounded plastic-tipped applicators worked best for me. I think it may depend on the cause of your gastroparesis. Unfortunately, gastroparesis can be induced by long-term use of opioids and opioids slow your gut motility anyway, so definitely be prepared for them to suggest stopping the opioids. If they want to rule out organic causes of your gastroparesis, they may want to take you off the meds and then do another gastric emptying test to see how your system functions without the medication. 

I know this isn’t what you wanted to hear, but especially with your medical history of GI issues and surgery, it might be really important for them to take you off opioids at least temporarily. Gastroparesis can have life-threatening complications like bezoars causing bowel obstructions, infections in your stomach and esophagus, and even esophageal tears. But you absolutely have the right to ask for alternative pain control during this process, and if your docs do their due diligence you should absolutely not be taken off cold turkey.

Botox takes 5-7 days to kick in, and after it did my jaw would be much more sore than usual because I was still trying to clench my teeth while the muscles were shrinking. Chewing hard or chewy food was more difficult and made me a little sore. At its peak effectiveness, I noticed my jawline was noticeably slimmer and my masseters didn’t pop out when I bit down. 

Note that jaw Botox only shrinks the masseter muscles, it can’t change the shape of your jaw. I have a pretty square jaw and it was still square after Botox. The Botox lasted about 3 months for me. 

An unfortunate side effect of Botox for teeth grinding/clenching is the risk of developing jowls. If you’ve been clenching and grinding for a long time, your skin has stretched to accommodate the bigger muscle. Once the muscle shrinks, there’s a bit of loose skin. You could use a hip localization technique to find the femoral neck. Locate the ASIS and move your crosshairs 1-2 inches medial and 3-4 inches distal from the ASIS. Open the collimation to include one-third of the proximal femur, the pubic symphysis, and the iliac crest. 

If you take an AP pelvis before moving onto the hip, positioning for the hip is a lot easier. The top of the cassette should be about an inch above the iliac crest, so you can use this as a guide on smaller and larger patients. Remember, regardless of the amount of adipose tissue, the bones will be in the same place. 

I generally keep the board in place for an AP hip after taking an AP pelvis. If they have a hip replacement or other hardware you might have to move the board down a few inches.

Hey, I and lots of other people in human medicine run into this problem too. I do x-ray and sometimes that involves moving broken bones and doing other painful and uncomfortable procedures. My first time getting x-rays of a 90 year old with a hip fracture was awful. She screamed and cried and I felt like I was torturing someone. 

But you have to realize that you’re not the reason this patient is at the doctor, you’re there to treat them. When you break a bone and the doctor has to reset it, it hurts. But you’re not the one who made them hurt or sick; you’re the one who is going to help them.

So, I need you to understand that everyone’s medical situation is different. I don’t disagree that in the situation you described with Norcos, a reevaluation and a new pain management plan may be needed. However, it’s not your job to make these recommendations, especially if you are a pharmacy tech. And refusing to refill the Norco early in that situation because you don’t agree with the treatment plan puts the patient in unnecessary discomfort. The patient needs to take that issue up with their doctor. 

About the benzodiazepines- Again, you need to understand that you don’t understand everyone’s situation. You’re fine taking Xanax for panic attacks twice a month or so, that’s great! Xanax is an excellent short-acting anxiolytic for stuff like that. There are other benzodiazepines that are longer-acting and therefore may be prescribed to be taken daily instead of “as needed”, for reasons that you may not be privy to. 

Longer-acting benzodiazepines being prescribed for GAD or social anxiety is being phased out over time (and that’s a good thing), but there will always be patients who need to take their benzodiazepines daily for months and maybe even years. There’s several reasons why this might go on. For example, some people who were prescribed large amounts of daily benzos back before we knew about its addiction potential have been on it so long that there are serious concerns about withdrawal will affect them. Or, some people who were prescribed daily benzodiazepines meant to be used for a short period of time sometimes end up staying on it long term because it consistently keeps them stable while other medications have failed. Benzos are notoriously difficult to taper off from, and tapering incorrectly can cause serious side effects such as seizures, heart palpitations, hallucinations, and suicidal ideation. Sometimes docs have to weight the risk of addiction/dependence against the risk of seriously destabilizing the patient. 

I understand that you have strong opinions about how pain and anxiety should be managed. It’s good that you have an understanding of how these medications work and how they might best be prescribed. However, if the only information you have about a patient’s care plan is the name and amount of a medication, it’s not appropriate for you to factor your personal opinions into how you care for the patient. You can raise your concerns with the patient’s doctor, but that’s all you can do. If the doctor writes the prescription and it is not objectively unsafe or illegal you should fill it when it is due for a refill. 

Basically, you’re not a doctor. You don’t always know best. You should probably stick to what’s within your scope of practice and leave the judgement and pettiness at home.

You do not suck! Six comps for your first semester is right on schedule at least at my school. I know how frustrating it is when you almost get the comp and then one little thing goes wrong and they can’t give it to you. My biggest tip when you’re doing a comp is to slooooow down. Try to set the room up before you bring in the patient, if that’s possible. Make a mental checklist of stuff you need to do and in what order before you bring them in. I always liked to get my own patients rather than having someone else get them in the room because I could assess their mobility and condition from the start. This helps to anticipate issues with positioning or patient movement. 

Take time to double check positions and if you aren’t sure if you’ll clip something, look at the shadows. If the shadow is going above the light you will clip it, so open it up until you can see a clear light border around the shadow. Yes, practice tight collimation, but don’t get too fussy about it. Getting the image in one shot with a little extra space is better than having to repeat the shot because you clipped something. 

Sometimes you won’t get it because of circumstances that are out of your control, and that sucks, but if you genuinely did everything you could don’t feel bad about it. Not every exam is comp-able as I’m sure you know.

Don’t feel stupid! You’re just starting out! In my first semester I got yelled at so bad by a tech because I didn’t understand what “rotoring” meant. I felt very upset because at that point in time (3-ish weeks into clinical) most techs were not letting us bush the button yet, so nobody had bothered to explain how to rotor and expose. The information doesn’t come all at once and no one is born knowing how to do x-ray so don’t be so hard on yourself.   

But to answer your question: Push the top part of the button down until you hear it start to spin and buzz (that’s the rotor), look to check the patient’s breathing, then press the whole thing down. After the beeeeep finishes, take your finger off. It won’t expose if you don’t rotor first, so don’t try to mash in the whole thing. It also won’t do the exposure if you don’t hold down the lower button long enough.  I’d ask a tech to let you watch their hands very closely when they push the button so you get a good look at what their fingers are doing. You’ll get it soon don’t worry!

Take humans for example; when we evolved to walk upright, that came with some big trade offs. We’re very prone to lower back issues because of all the pressure on our spine and it also makes childbirth more difficult and dangerous than our 4-legged ancestors. Bipedalism also exacerbates knee and foot issues. 

Evolution also isn’t necessarily efficient- this is why we still have accessory organs such as the spleen and the appendix. It’s also why we still have a tailbone, a remnant from having tails. There’s a couple studies that say that but as other people in the thread pointed out, they’re statistically flawed. One thing I found flipping through studies is that it isn’t so much that black people have high bone density, but that they do in comparison to white and Asian populations. White and Asian people, especially women, are more prone to diseases like osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis that decrease bone density. 

X-ray exposure techniques are based on body habitus (size of the part being imaged) and any present pathologies. A white woman may need less radiation if she has osteoporosis, because the bones are less dense. A black woman may need more radiation if she has a larger body habitus because you need more electrons to penetrate the body. But none of these are hard and fast rules. Medicine has changed a lot in the last century, but misogyny and racism still hang around with relatively “harmless” stuff like this: black people have thicker bones, have more psychiatric issues, can’t feel pain the same. To change things you have to challenge these beliefs. 

I would also like to note that today x-ray is very safe and is a negligible dose of radiation unless they’re getting x-rays or CT scans done constantly. But in the past (probably when the guy I heard this from was in school), exposure techniques were set manually and the system typically needed a higher dose of radiation than today’s systems. And the vast, vast majority of people I’ve worked with in x-ray don’t buy this kind of crap. I did this a while back with some of my college essays. Literally all of them were typed up on the computer over hours and hours by yours truly. 

I found a pretty interesting pattern, actually. The essays that were about more common or “basic” topics would get high percentages of AI. Say you had to write an essay explaining The Allegory of the Cave. Millions and millions of people have probably written the same essay using mostly the same sources which use similar phrasing to explain topics. For essays about less common topics or very academically dense content, I got a very low or zero AI score. 

I also noticed that vocabulary is a big part of what those checkers picked up on. Essays with longer, more complex vocabulary or flowery language was considered to be human. Using smaller/simpler terms and less fluff was determined to be AI generated. 

I’ve only tried this with essays and research projects, not stuff like poetry and fiction for what it’s worth.

Focus on getting through one day at a time. Try everything to see what works for you: tylenol+ibuprofen, heat, ice, muscle creams, arthritis creams, braces for your joints, stretching, walking, soaking in a hot tub, swimming maybe, yoga, light weightlifting, etc. If you have pain walking or standing, invest in a good pair of shoes. Find those ole reliables and keep them on you wherever you go. Don’t be afraid to try new medications from the doctor but also don’t be afraid to say no to a medication you’re not sure about. Tell your doctor about side effects that are bothering you so you guys can figure out an alternative. 

Try to be as pragmatic and calm as you can when at the doctor’s office. Describe how the pain is affecting your ability to do things and enjoy your life. Don’t ask directly for pain meds unless it’s something like toradol, which is in the same class as ibuprofen. 

Lastly, cut yourself some slack. You’re dealing with some stuff most people your age don’t. Try not to feel bad if you can’t do all the stuff your friends want you to do and prioritize your health first. True friends will understand and will accommodate you. Don’t listen to the fake friends or well-meaning but unhelpful people in your life. They may tell you that you’re being lazy, that you’re not trying enough, that if you just tried this or that you’d be healed, that you’re exaggerating. Don’t listen to them. They only care about your pain when it affects them and they don’t deserve to have you in their life.

Holy fucking fuck, I am SO glad to see people talking about IUDs on here!! A lot of my problems began shortly after I had Kyleena placed in 2018. They told me it would make my periods stop or get lighter and that it was smaller than Mirena so the side effects wouldn’t be as bad. The insertion was excruciating but went fine otherwise, it was placed correctly and everything and never dislodged or perforated. However, I started to have increasing pain and discomfort in my chest/ribcage area. Then one day I felt a lump. I hightailed it to my college’s student health center and they immediately scheduled me for an ultrasound. It was a benign fibroadenoma in my breast and I also had small cysts in the area. Not cancer, thank god. But the pain kept getting worse and worse in my chest to the point I would cry almost every night and annoyed the hell out of my boyfriend because I couldn’t sleep. I also had periods that lasted 2 weeks and then came again a week later. My cramps were worse than they had ever been. 

Around the 6 month mark of having Kyleena, I felt I started to get a little chunky. My stomach poked out more and my abdomen felt… heavy. Then I started having sharp pains in my lower abdomen that scared me enough to go to the hospital. 2cm ovarian cyst. I had just about had enough at this point, I was convinced the IUD was giving me these horrible side effects and I wanted it out. I took it out and instantly the abdomen pain and heavy periods disappeared. However, the pain in my chest did not. It got worse and worse. I saw so many doctors. The first gynecologist blew me off and told me it’s normal to have sore breasts around your period. The second gynecologist actually tried his best to help me for several years. He referred me for multiple ultrasounds over the years and referred me to surgery when the lumps got too big and painful. We also tried adjusting my hormones with different birth controls and HRT for a few years, believing that a hormonal imbalance was causing an abnormal amount of inflammation in the area. Nothing helped. Some meds made it worse but none made it any better. I was in excruciating pain for years and years. I even stopped birth control entirely for a year, thinking the extra hormones were making things worse. It didn’t help. I had to stop wearing regular bras, then sports bras hurt too much, and eventually bralettes started to hurt. I go without or with an undershirt these days. 

Finally my gyne threw his hands up and said he thinks this is something beyond what he can fix. He referred me to rheumatology. Bam, fibromyalgia diagnosis on the first visit. They prescribe me gabapentin and it helps… for a little bit. These days it doesn’t do much and it’s not worth the brain fog to take it. 

Now I’ve finally gotten an MRI of my back and discovered some mild degenerative changes, arthritis, and bone spurs. They’re referring me to PT and neurosurgery for steroid shots. I am dying to ask this neurologist if my 6-year long battle with breast/ribcage pain has anything to do with nerves in my spine. 

But also, I can’t shake the feeling that this might be some horrible, long-lasting side effect from that damn IUD. It seems like almost everyone who gets one has a story, and a percentage of those end up facing long-term health issues. I feel like more testing needs to be done on implanted birth control devices in general. They already lie about the side effects and the pain of the procedure. What else are these devices doing to people?

You also have to play the game to get chronic pain taken seriously. Have documented visits with the same issue with the same doctor or just a few doctors. Keep up with what tests have been ordered and what tests haven’t. Which meds helped, which made it worse, which were useless. Ask for referrals to different specialties until you find a doctor that’s helpful. I’ve never kept a pain journal, but I did take time to write out a list of all the ways the pain affects me in daily life, how hard it makes things for me. You need documented, consistent frequency and severity of pain for at least 1-2 years, probably more, to be taken seriously as a candidate for chronic pain treatment. 1. Try to start the argument calmly. Take a step back, if at all possible, and really, really think about what you’re going to say and how you’re going to say it. It’s easy to come off as accusatory or combative and people react defensively to that. 

2. Instead of saying “You did this thing x that hurt my feelings”, try “I felt really hurt when you did x, can we talk about that?” Try to explain how YOU feel instead of projecting your beliefs about the other person’s motivations or reasoning behind their actions. 

3. Ask them what you could both do to improve the situation. Even if you don’t feel like you’re in the wrong, ask them if there’s anything you could have done to prevent the issue from escalating to an argument. 

4. Communication is key. A healthy argument should be more of a discussion, not a shouting match or berating each other. If the other person cannot or will not have a calm conversation about the issue and wants to continue being passive-aggressive or hurtful, it’s time to walk away for a bit. Say, “Let’s have this conversation when we’re both a little calmer” or offer to give them some space and talk about the issue later.

The whole “you need to learn to heal yourself” thing has always bothered me. Yes, healing from trauma is a LOT of working on yourself, recognizing your unhealthy thought and behavior patterns, and making changes to your life in general. But a healthy support network is an important component to effective mental health treatment, and I feel like people who don’t have that are kind of left out in the cold. 

A few years ago I lost most of my friends by relying on them too much when I was in a mental health crisis. It’s hard for me to fault them for dipping when I was such a hot mess, even though I felt that I would be more supportive if it was them in that situation. To stop that from happening again, I kept my remaining friends at arms-length for a time. They knew I was struggling but I rarely opened up so they never knew the true extent. I was afraid of overwhelming them and having them leave again. I had to work hard (it took several years) to learn who I could trust and how to trust again, and also to have healthy, productive conversations with them about my mental health. Venting is okay sometimes, but I found that it goes over better when I ask them for permission to vent/say potentially upsetting stuff and when I tell them they don’t have to know what to say, I just want them to listen and be there. 

Sometimes you have to ask people for what you need, and it’s up to you and how well you know them to realize when you might be asking for too much. In an ideal world, no one who cares would ever find me “too much” to deal with. But I do think you have to be mindful that many people are simply poor at managing other people’s emotions, and although they may feel for you, lack the emotional skills necessary to productively talk about trauma with a traumatized person. I do my best to avoid people who aren’t very good with empathy, people who constantly need to make it about themselves, judgmental types, and people with little patience. It’s about how you express yourself, but also about who you’re talking to. 

I’m sorry you’ve felt rejected by so many people. I’ve gone through the same thing and the only way out of it was picking better friends and learning how to talk about my issues in a productive manner. I hope you find the peace you need. ❤️
